{{short description|Theorem regarding circulation in a barotropic ideal fluid}}

In [[fluid mechanics]], '''Kelvin's circulation theorem''' states:<ref>Kundu, P and Cohen, I: ''Fluid Mechanics'', page 130. Academic Press 2002</ref><ref>Katz, Plotkin: ''Low-Speed Aerodynamics''</ref><blockquote>In a [[barotropic]], [[ideal fluid]] with [[Conservative force|conservative]] body forces, the [[Circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]] around a closed curve (which encloses the same fluid elements) moving with the fluid remains constant with time.</blockquote>

The theorem is named after [[William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin]] who published it in 1869.

Stated mathematically:

:<math>\frac{\mathrm{D}\Gamma}{\mathrm{D}t} = 0</math>

where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]] around a material moving contour <math>C(t)</math> as a function of time <math>t</math>. The differential operator <math>\mathrm{D}</math> is a substantial (material) derivative moving with the fluid particles.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://web.mit.edu/fluids-modules/www/potential_flows/LecturesHTML/lec07/kelvintheoproof/kelvintheoproof.html |access-date=3 June 2024 |title=Proof of Kelvin's Theorem (From JNN, page 103) [Marine Hydrodynamics, Fall 2003 Lecture 7] |website=web.mit.edu/fluids-modules |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Department of Ocean Engineering |first=Karl P. |last=Burr |date=2003-07-07 }}</ref> Stated more simply, this theorem says that if one observes a closed contour at one instant, and follows the contour over time (by following the motion of all of its fluid elements), the circulation over the two locations of this contour remains constant.

This theorem does not hold in cases with [[viscous]] stresses, nonconservative body forces (for example the [[Coriolis force]]) or non-barotropic pressure-density relations.

In the simplifying special case of [[steady flow]] the theorem can be applied to a closed curve that has a fixed position so that fluid elements flow through the closed curve. In the study of airfoils producing lift, it is often instructive to examine the circulation around any closed curve that fully encloses the airfoil; in the steady flow of an inviscid fluid past a stationary airfoil, the theorem can be applied to this closed curve.<ref>Anderson, John D. (1984) ''Fundamentals of Aerodynamics'', Section 4.6, McGraw-Hill Inc.</ref>

==Mathematical proof==
{{see also|Euler equations (fluid dynamics)}}
The circulation <math>\Gamma</math> around a closed material contour <math>C(t)</math> is defined by:
:<math>\Gamma(t) = \oint_C \boldsymbol{u} \cdot \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s}</math>
where '''''u''''' is the velocity vector, and '''''ds''''' is an element along the closed contour.

The governing equation for an inviscid fluid with a conservative [[body force]] is
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{u}}{\mathrm{D} t} = - \frac{1}{\rho}\boldsymbol{\nabla}p + \boldsymbol{\nabla} \Phi</math>
where D/D''t'' is the [[convective derivative]], ''ρ'' is the fluid density, ''p'' is the pressure and ''Φ'' is the potential for the body force. These are the Euler equations with a body force.

The condition of barotropicity implies that the density is a function only of the pressure, i.e. <math>\rho=\rho(p)</math>.

Taking the convective derivative of circulation gives
:<math> \frac{\mathrm{D}\Gamma}{\mathrm{D} t} = \oint_C \frac{\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{u}}{\mathrm{D}t} \cdot \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s} + \oint_C \boldsymbol{u} \cdot  \frac{\mathrm{D} \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s}}{\mathrm{D}t}. </math>

For the first term, we substitute from the governing equation, and then apply [[Stokes' theorem]], thus:
:<math> \oint_C \frac{\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{u}}{\mathrm{D}t} \cdot \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s} = \int_A \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \left( -\frac{1}{\rho} \boldsymbol{\nabla} p + \boldsymbol{\nabla} \Phi \right) \cdot \boldsymbol{n} \, \mathrm{d}S =  \int_A \frac{1}{\rho^2} \left( \boldsymbol{\nabla} \rho \times \boldsymbol{\nabla} p \right) \cdot \boldsymbol{n} \, \mathrm{d}S = 0. </math>
The final equality arises since <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \rho \times \boldsymbol{\nabla} p=0</math> owing to barotropicity. We have also made use of the fact that the curl of any gradient is necessarily 0, or <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \boldsymbol{\nabla} f=0</math> for any function <math>f</math>.

For the second term, we note that evolution of the material [[line element]] is given by
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{D} \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s}}{\mathrm{D}t} = \left( \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla} \right) \boldsymbol{u}.</math>
Hence
:<math>\oint_C \boldsymbol{u} \cdot  \frac{\mathrm{D} \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s}}{\mathrm{D}t} = \oint_C \boldsymbol{u} \cdot \left( \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla} \right) \boldsymbol{u} = \frac{1}{2} \oint_C \boldsymbol{\nabla} \left( |\boldsymbol{u}|^2 \right) \cdot \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s} = 0.</math>
The last equality is obtained by applying [[gradient theorem]].

Since both terms are zero, we obtain the result
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{D}\Gamma}{\mathrm{D}t} = 0.</math>

== Poincaré–Bjerknes circulation theorem ==
A similar principle which conserves a quantity can be obtained for the rotating frame also, known as the Poincaré–Bjerknes theorem, named after [[Henri Poincaré]] and [[Vilhelm Bjerknes]], who derived the invariant in 1893<ref>Poincaré, H. (1893). Théorie des tourbillons: Leçons professées pendant le deuxième semestre 1891-92 (Vol. 11). Gauthier-Villars. Article 158</ref><ref>Truesdell, C. (2018). The kinematics of vorticity. Courier Dover Publications.</ref> and 1898.<ref>Bjerknes, V., Rubenson, R., & Lindstedt, A. (1898). Ueber einen Hydrodynamischen Fundamentalsatz und seine Anwendung: besonders auf die Mechanik der Atmosphäre und des Weltmeeres. Kungl. Boktryckeriet. PA Norstedt & Söner.</ref><ref>Chandrasekhar, S. (2013). Hydrodynamic and hydromagnetic stability. Courier Corporation.</ref> The theorem can be applied to a rotating frame which is rotating at a constant [[angular velocity]] given by the vector <math> \boldsymbol{\Omega} </math>, for the modified circulation

:<math>\Gamma(t) = \oint_C (\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \boldsymbol{r}) \cdot \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{s}</math>

Here <math> \boldsymbol{r} </math> is the position of the area of fluid. From [[Stokes' theorem]], this is:

:<math>\Gamma(t) = \int_A \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times  (\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \boldsymbol{r}) \cdot \boldsymbol{n} \, \mathrm{d}S =  \int_A (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \boldsymbol{u} + 2 \boldsymbol{\Omega}) \cdot \boldsymbol{n} \, \mathrm{d}S</math>

The [[vorticity]] of a velocity field in fluid dynamics is defined by:

:<math>\boldsymbol{\omega} = \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \boldsymbol{u}</math>

Then:

:<math>\Gamma(t) = \int_A (\boldsymbol{\omega} + 2 \boldsymbol{\Omega}) \cdot \boldsymbol{n} \, \mathrm{d}S</math>
